meta_title: Thirty Words That Mark a Serious Aroid Collector
meta_description: A field lexicon of the rare-plant trade — from jump to wet stick to pup — and what the vocabulary reveals about the people using it.
title: The Quiet Vocabulary of the Rare Plant Room
deck: Thirty terms that separate a working collector from a hobbyist with a wishlist — and what each one actually means.
intro: The first time someone offers you a wet stick, you should not be alarmed. You should ask what node count, whether it has roots, and what mother plant it came off. If you answer correctly, the seller relaxes a little. You have passed a small test you didn't know you were taking.

Every serious hobby develops a private language, and rare aroids are no exception. The vocabulary that has grown up around _Philodendron_, _Anthurium_, and _Monstera_ collecting is part Latin nomenclature, part horticulture, and part eBay slang from 2019. Used well, it's precise. Used badly, it sounds like a teenager trying to buy a car. What follows is a working glossary — not exhaustive, but enough to read a Facebook group thread without embarrassing yourself, and enough to spot the seller who's bluffing.

sections.heading: Propagation: jump, pup, wet stick, chonk
paragraphs: A **cutting** is the broadest term — any severed piece of stem with at least one node, the swollen ring from which roots and leaves emerge. Beyond that, the vocabulary gets oddly specific. A **wet stick** is an unrooted node cutting, usually leafless or nearly so, sold cheap because the buyer is taking on the risk that it will actually wake up. A **chonk** is the same idea but bigger: a thick, multi-node piece of mature stem, often from a climbing _Philodendron_ that has already hardened off and started producing adult foliage. Chonks cost more and root faster.

A **pup** is an offset — a young plant growing from the base of a clumping species. _Anthurium warocqueanum_ throws pups eventually if it's happy; so do most _Alocasia_. **Division** is the act of separating those pups from the mother, ideally with their own root system intact. A **jump** is more colloquial: a leaf that comes in dramatically larger than the previous one, the visual proof that a plant has decided, finally, that it likes where it lives. Collectors post jumps the way other people post their kids' report cards.

**Acclimation** is the period — anywhere from two weeks to two months — during which a new arrival adjusts to your conditions. **Hardening off** is the related process of moving a plant from high-humidity propagation (a tent, a tub, a bag) into open room air without it collapsing. Both are skills. Neither is glamorous.

sections.heading: Provenance: NOID, sib cross, tissue culture, line
paragraphs: **NOID** stands for No Identification — a plant of uncertain species, often a hybrid or a wild collection that never got matched to a type specimen. NOID _Anthurium_ from Ecuador are their own category of obsession; people pay real money for what amounts to a botanical question mark. **Aff.** (short for _affinis_) means "close to but not confirmed as" a named species. **Sp.** means "species, undetermined." Both are honest hedges. **Cf.** (_confer_) means "compare with" — a similar hedge used by people who know what they're looking at but won't commit.

A **sib cross** is a sibling crossing — two plants from the same seed batch crossed back to each other. **Selfed** means a plant pollinated with its own pollen. Both produce variable offspring, which is why two _Philodendron spiritus-sancti_ seedlings from the same pod can look noticeably different at maturity. A **line** or **bloodline** refers to a specific lineage maintained by a particular grower; certain _Anthurium luxurians_ lines, for example, have larger bullation or deeper venation than others.

**TC** is tissue culture — plants propagated in sterile flasks from meristem tissue. TC plants are cheaper, available in volume, and sometimes carry juvenile traits for longer than cutting-grown stock. **Cutting-grown** or **stem-grown** stock comes from a known mother plant and reaches maturity faster. Neither is inherently better, but the distinction matters when you're spending three figures on a small plant.

sections.heading: Morphology: bullate, sinus, peduncle, geniculum
paragraphs: This is where the vocabulary gets unforgiving. **Bullate** means blistered or puckered — the quilted leaf surface of _Anthurium luxurians_ or a good _Begonia melanobullata_. **Velvet** or **velutinous** describes the matte, light-absorbing texture of _Philodendron melanochrysum_ and _gloriosum_. **Crystalline** or **sparkly** is the iridescent surface of _Anthurium crystallinum_ and _clarinervium_, caused by specialized epidermal cells that catch light.

The **sinus** is the gap at the base of a heart-shaped leaf, where the two lobes meet (or don't). On a mature _Philodendron gloriosum_ the sinus is open and rounded; on a _Philodendron pastazanum_ it closes up tight, lobes overlapping. The **petiole** is the leaf stem. Its cross-section is diagnostic: a D-shaped, winged, or terete petiole can settle an identification argument that photos of the leaf cannot.

The **geniculum** is the small joint where petiole meets leaf blade — the hinge that lets the leaf reorient toward light. On _Anthurium_, geniculum length and color are taxonomically useful. The **peduncle** is the stalk holding up an inflorescence; the **spathe** is the modified leaf that wraps it; the **spadix** is the fleshy column of true flowers inside. If you intend to pollinate anything, you will learn all three within a week.

sections.heading: Variegation: stable, sectoral, chimeric, reverted
paragraphs: **Variegation** is the general term for any pattern of non-green tissue — white, cream, yellow, pink — caused by reduced or absent chlorophyll. **Chimeric** variegation, the kind that matters, is genetic: two distinct cell lines in the same plant, inherited through cuttings if you take them correctly. The albo _Monstera_, the mint _Monstera_, the _Philodendron_ 'Pink Princess' — all chimeric.

**Sectoral** variegation comes in clean wedges or halves; **marginal** runs along the leaf edge; **mosaic** scatters in fine flecks. A **half-moon** is a leaf split roughly fifty-fifty between green and white tissue — beautiful, but a warning sign if it keeps happening, because the white half has no chlorophyll and the plant is running on the green half alone. A **destabilized** or **reverted** plant has lost its variegation, usually because someone propagated from an all-green section.

**Viral variegation** is the exception — patterns caused by a plant virus rather than genetics, sometimes attractive, always contagious, never worth buying. The classic case is the so-called _Aglaonema_ 'Pictum Tricolor' counterfeits, but viral mottling shows up across the trade. If a pattern looks like watercolor bleed rather than crisp sectors, ask questions.

sections.heading: Conditions: VPD, IBC, LECA, semi-hydro
paragraphs: **VPD** is vapor pressure deficit — the difference between how much moisture the air is holding and how much it could hold at that temperature. It's a more useful number than relative humidity alone, because a plant at 80% humidity and 60°F is in a very different situation from one at 80% humidity and 80°F. Serious growers chase a VPD around 0.8 to 1.2 kPa for most aroids.

An **IBC** is an intermediate bulk container — those big white cube tanks in metal cages, sawed in half and converted into walk-in propagation chambers. **Pon**, **LECA**, and **lava rock** are inorganic substrates used in **semi-hydro** setups, where the plant sits in inert media with a reservoir of nutrient solution below. Semi-hydro reduces root rot in plants that resent wet organic media — many _Anthurium_, in particular — but it asks you to learn fertilizer chemistry.

**Airy mix** is the catchall term for a chunky, fast-draining substrate: bark, perlite, pumice, charcoal, sometimes coco chunks or sphagnum. The exact recipe is a religion. What matters is that water moves through it freely and roots get oxygen between waterings. Soggy peat kills more rare aroids than any pest.

sections.heading: The social vocabulary: grail, FOMO flip, OG, on the hunt
paragraphs: Then there are the words that aren't about plants at all. A **grail** is the species you've been chasing for years — for some collectors it's _Philodendron spiritus-sancti_, for others a true _Anthurium dressleri_ or a wild-collected _Monstera obliqua_ Peru. A **holy grail** is a grail you no longer expect to own. **On the hunt** means actively looking, usually publicly, in the hope that someone will surface a cutting.

A **FOMO flip** is buying a plant at the top of its hype cycle and reselling it before the market corrects — the _Philodendron_ 'Pink Princess' market in 2021, the _Monstera_ 'Thai Constellation' market in 2022. **OG** marks an early import or a long-established clone, as opposed to a newer TC release. **Mother** is the plant you cut from; **pieces** are what you sell off her.

The vocabulary is a filter. It tells you, within about ninety seconds, whether the person on the other end of the DM has actually grown the plant or whether they're moving boxes from a wholesaler in Florida. Both transactions are legitimate. They are not the same transaction. Learning the words is how you tell the difference — and, eventually, how you stop being the one being filtered.
